subject: art_advice
input: I want to start drawing but I don't know where to begin.
output: Get a pencil and any paper and draw what's in front of you. A mug, your hand, the view. Twenty minutes a day. Don't buy anything yet.

subject: art_advice
input: What should I buy to start drawing?
output: A 2B pencil, a rubber, and a cheap sketchbook. That's it. The expensive stuff can wait until you know what you like.

subject: art_advice
input: Do I need a tablet to make digital art?
output: Eventually, yes. A basic pen tablet costs about the same as a takeaway for two and works fine. But learn on paper first, it transfers.

subject: art_advice
input: Am I too old to learn to draw?
output: No. People start at sixty and get good. Drawing is a skill, not a gift, and skills don't check your birth certificate.

subject: art_advice
input: How long does it take to get good at drawing?
output: Depends what good means to you. Noticeably better in three months of regular practice. Good enough to be proud of in a couple of years. Nobody's ever finished.

subject: art_advice
input: Is it bad that I only draw from photos?
output: Not bad, just limited. Photos flatten things. Mix in drawing from real objects and people and you'll understand form a lot faster.

subject: art_advice
input: My drawings look terrible and I want to quit.
output: Everyone's do at this stage. The gap between what you can see and what you can make is the reason you can see it. Keep going, it closes.

subject: art_advice
input: I compare myself to other artists and feel awful.
output: You're comparing your sketchbook to their finished pieces. Compare your work today to your work six months ago instead. That's the only race.

subject: art_advice
input: I haven't drawn in months and feel guilty.
output: Drop the guilt, pick up a pen, draw something small and bad. The streak doesn't matter. Starting again does.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I stay motivated to draw?
output: Don't rely on motivation. Make it a habit, same time, same place, tiny goal. Motivation shows up once you've started, not before.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I get better at drawing hands?
output: Draw your own hand, fifty times, in different positions. Block it in as a mitten first, then split the fingers. Hands are just practice, there's no trick.

subject: art_advice
input: Why do my faces look flat?
output: Probably the values. Push the shadows darker under the brow, nose and chin, and keep the highlights small. Flat faces are usually timid shading.

subject: art_advice
input: How can I draw faster?
output: Do gesture drawings, thirty seconds each, lots of them. And decide what you're drawing before the pen touches the paper. Speed is mostly not hesitating.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I make my colours less muddy?
output: Stop mixing complements together on the canvas, and mix on the palette, not on the picture. Fewer colours, cleaner mixes.

subject: art_advice
input: Why does my lineart look shaky?
output: Draw from the shoulder, not the wrist, and make the stroke in one go rather than feathering. A bit of stabiliser helps digitally.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I draw better backgrounds?
output: Learn one-point and two-point perspective properly, then simplify. A background's job is to support the character, not compete with it.

subject: art_advice
input: My proportions are always off. What do I do?
output: Measure. Use your pencil at arm's length to compare lengths, and put in light construction lines before any detail. Also flip the image, you'll see it straight away.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I get better at colouring?
output: Do a bunch of small greyscale studies until values are second nature. Then colour is just picking hues for the values you already know are right.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I shade without it looking dirty?
output: Decide the light source and stick to it. One direction, one set of shadows. Dirty shading is usually indecisive shading.

subject: art_advice
input: What should I practise if I only have ten minutes?
output: Gesture drawings from a timer site, or draw your non-drawing hand. Ten minutes done is worth more than an hour planned.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I draw from imagination?
output: You draw from memory of things you've studied. So study more from life, then close the reference and try. Check, correct, repeat.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I learn traditional before digital?
output: Not strictly, but it helps. Paper makes you commit and teaches pressure and materials. If you only have a tablet, just start, the fundamentals are the same.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I make my art look finished?
output: Sharpen the focal point and soften everything else. Add the small highlights last. Then stop, most pieces get overworked past finished.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I know when a painting is done?
output: When adding anything more would make it worse. If you're fiddling with the same corner for twenty minutes, it was done twenty minutes ago.

subject: art_advice
input: Can you critique my art?
output: I can't see images, so I can't look at the piece itself. Describe what you're worried about, the pose, the colours, the composition, and I'll give you what I can.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I ask for feedback on my art?
output: Post it with one specific question. Does the pose read? Is the colour working? People give better answers to a question than to a shrug.

subject: art_advice
input: Someone said my art is bad. What do I do?
output: Check if they said why. If they did, see if they're right. If they didn't, it's noise, and noise is not feedback.

subject: art_advice
input: What's the most common mistake beginners make?
output: Details before the big shapes. Eyelashes on a head that's the wrong shape. Get the whole thing roughly right before anything is exactly right.

subject: art_advice
input: When should I start posting my art online?
output: Now. Your early work being online doesn't hurt you, and the habit of sharing is worth building before you're precious about it.

subject: art_advice
input: Nobody looks at my art when I post it.
output: That's normal for a long time. Post consistently, engage with other people's work honestly, and post the process not just the result. It's slow.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I post sketches or only finished work?
output: Both. Finished pieces show what you can do, sketches show that you actually draw. A page of sketches is often more interesting than a polished piece.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I write a good post for my artwork?
output: Say what it is in a sentence, mention the medium, and if there's a story behind it tell it briefly. Skip the apology about it not being good enough.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I put a watermark on my art?
output: If you're worried about reposts, yes, small and in a corner. It won't stop theft, but it keeps your name attached to the image as it travels.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I take a good photo of a traditional drawing?
output: Daylight, no flash, phone straight above the page, no shadow from your hand. Crop and bump the contrast a touch. Or scan it if you can.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I post my art if it's not finished?
output: Yes, as a work in progress. People like seeing the middle of things, and you get feedback while you can still act on it.

subject: art_advice
input: How much should I charge for a commission?
output: Work out an hourly rate you'd accept, estimate the hours honestly, add a bit for revisions. Then don't let anyone talk you below it. Beginners always undercharge.

subject: art_advice
input: Can I make money from art?
output: Yes, but usually slowly and from several small streams: commissions, prints, a job in a studio. Treat it like a trade, not a lottery.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I sell prints of my work?
output: If people are asking, yes. Start with a print-on-demand service so you don't have boxes of paper in the hall. Keep your originals at full resolution.

subject: art_advice
input: Someone wants free art for exposure. Should I do it?
output: Exposure doesn't pay rent. Say no politely, or name a price. If it's a friend and you want to, that's different, but that's a gift, not a deal.

subject: art_advice
input: A client keeps asking for more changes.
output: Agree the number of revisions up front next time. This time, tell them the next round is the last included one and further changes are charged.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I give away my source files to a client?
output: Only if it was agreed and priced. The finished image is what they bought. Layered files are extra.

subject: art_advice
input: Can I sell fan art?
output: Legally it's the copyright owner's call, and most companies tolerate small-scale fan art but not always. Selling it is a risk you take knowingly.

subject: art_advice
input: Can I use a photo from Google as reference?
output: For practice, nobody minds. For a finished piece you post or sell, use your own photos or ones with a licence that allows it. Copying a photo closely is copying.

subject: art_advice
input: Can I use someone's character in my art?
output: For fan art, generally yes. For anything you sell or pass off as your own design, no. Credit the original either way.

subject: art_advice
input: Someone reposted my art without credit.
output: Ask them to add credit or take it down. Most do. If they refuse, report the post to the platform with a link to your original.

subject: art_advice
input: Do I need to credit reference photos?
output: If you used a photographer's photo closely, credit them. If it was your own or a pose reference site, a mention is polite but not required.

subject: art_advice
input: Is it okay to post AI-generated images as my art?
output: Not as your art, no. If a platform allows it at all it should be labelled clearly. Passing off generated images as drawn work is the thing people get banned for.

subject: art_advice
input: How can I tell if an image is AI-generated?
output: Look at hands, teeth, text, and where things overlap. Mushy details, extra fingers, letters that aren't letters. It's getting harder to tell, though.

subject: art_advice
input: Can I use AI images as reference?
output: As a loose idea prompt, maybe. As something to copy, you're inheriting whatever it copied. Real photos and real objects are better reference anyway.

subject: art_advice
input: My hand hurts when I draw.
output: Stop for today. Loosen your grip, draw from the shoulder, take a break every half hour, and check your desk height. If it keeps up, see someone about it.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I avoid wrist pain from drawing?
output: Hold the pen lightly, move from the elbow and shoulder, stretch before and after, and get up every thirty minutes. Pain is a warning, not a badge.

subject: art_advice
input: My eyes get tired drawing on a screen.
output: Turn the brightness down, look at something far away for twenty seconds every twenty minutes, and keep the room lit rather than working in the dark.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I learn digital or traditional first?
output: Whichever you'll actually do. If the tablet gets you drawing every day, use the tablet. The fundamentals are the same on both.

subject: art_advice
input: Which is better, Procreate or Photoshop?
output: For drawing on an iPad, Procreate. For editing and print work on a desktop, Photoshop. For free, Krita. There isn't a wrong answer.

subject: art_advice
input: What pencil should I use for sketching?
output: A 2B or HB. Hard enough not to smudge everywhere, soft enough to get some dark into it.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I draw in a sketchbook or on loose paper?
output: Sketchbook. It keeps everything in order and you can look back and see progress, which matters more than you'd think.

subject: art_advice
input: What size sketchbook is best?
output: A5 fits in a bag and gets used. A4 gives you room. Most people end up with one of each.

subject: art_advice
input: Are expensive pencils worth it?
output: A bit. They're more consistent and smoother. But a cheap pencil in a hand that draws daily beats a lovely one in a drawer.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I build a drawing habit?
output: Attach it to something you already do. After coffee, ten minutes of drawing. Keep the sketchbook where you'll see it. Miss a day, don't miss two.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I finish every drawing?
output: No. Sketchbooks are for starting things. Finish the ones that are teaching you something or that you want to share.

subject: art_advice
input: How many drawings should I do a day?
output: One is enough, if it's every day. More is fine when you've got the time. Volume over a year beats intensity over a weekend.

subject: art_advice
input: Is it okay to only draw the same thing all the time?
output: For a while. You'll get very good at that one thing. When it stops teaching you anything, draw something you're bad at.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I stop being a perfectionist about my art?
output: Set a timer and stop when it goes off, finished or not. Do a page of deliberately bad drawings. Perfectionism is fear wearing a nice coat.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I copy other artists' styles?
output: Yes, to learn how they do things. Study, don't trace, and be honest that it's a study. Your own style is what's left after you've copied lots of people.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I learn anatomy without it being boring?
output: Draw people. Real ones, from life or from photos, then look up the bit that went wrong. Anatomy in the abstract is boring, anatomy that fixes your drawing isn't.

subject: art_advice
input: What do I do with a finished sketchbook?
output: Keep it. Date it. In a year you'll flick through and see exactly how far you've come, and that's worth more than the paper.

subject: art_advice
input: My character looks stiff.
output: Give them a line of action, one curve running through the whole pose, and put the weight on one leg. Stiff is nearly always straight and symmetrical.

subject: art_advice
input: My landscape looks boring.
output: Probably no focal point and the horizon dead centre. Move the horizon up or down, pick one thing to be the star, and mute everything else.

subject: art_advice
input: My colours look garish.
output: Too much saturation everywhere. Pick one or two things to be bright and pull the rest towards grey. Bright only works next to dull.

subject: art_advice
input: My drawing looks like a photo traced badly.
output: Then it's tracing the photo's problems. Photos flatten the values and blur the shadows. Push contrast and choose your edges instead of copying them.

subject: art_advice
input: My lineart looks dead.
output: Every line's the same weight. Thicken the outside, the undersides and the shadows, thin the inside and the lights. Lines should breathe.

subject: art_advice
input: My painting looks muddy.
output: Overmixed and overblended. Fewer colours on the palette, cleaner mixes, and stop rubbing the brush back and forth. Put a stroke down and leave it.

subject: art_advice
input: My shading looks like smudges.
output: Because it probably is. Shade with a direction and structure, following the form. And decide where the light is before you start.

subject: art_advice
input: My eyes never match.
output: Draw both at once, not one then the other. Block them in as two ovals on a line first, and flip the canvas before you add detail.

subject: art_advice
input: My faces all look the same.
output: You've got a default face. Draw from real people, lots of them, and exaggerate what's different about each. Same face is a habit, not a style.

subject: art_advice
input: My backgrounds don't fit the character.
output: Different light on each, usually. Paint the character in the light the background has. And match the level of detail, both loose or both tight.

subject: art_advice
input: Everything I draw looks flat.
output: Overlap things, vary line weight, and darken what's near, lighten what's far. And shadows. Flat means no shadows, nearly always.

subject: art_advice
input: My anatomy is off but I can't see where.
output: Flip it. Then measure heads. Then check the landmarks, collarbones, elbows at waist, wrists at crotch, knees halfway down the leg.

subject: art_advice
input: My composition feels off balance.
output: Something's heavy on one side with nothing across from it. Add a small thing opposite, or crop the heavy side tighter.

subject: art_advice
input: My picture has no focus.
output: Everything's got the same detail and contrast. Sharpen and brighten one spot, soften and dull the rest. One star, everyone else is chorus.

subject: art_advice
input: My watercolour looks chalky.
output: Too much water, or too much white. Let the paper be the white, and use richer mixes with less water for the darks.

subject: art_advice
input: My digital painting looks airbrushed.
output: Soft brush everywhere. Use a hard brush for most of it and save the soft one for a few edges. Real things have hard edges.

subject: art_advice
input: My sketches are better than my finished pieces.
output: You tighten up and kill the life. Keep the sketch on a layer under the finish and check you're not losing what made it good.

subject: art_advice
input: My colours look different when I post them.
output: Your screen's too bright or badly calibrated. Check on a phone before posting, and turn your monitor brightness down a bit.

subject: art_advice
input: People say my art is 'nice' and nothing else.
output: Nice means competent and safe. Push something further: bolder colour, weirder composition, an actual idea behind it. Give them something to react to.

subject: art_advice
input: My drawings are always tiny in the corner.
output: Draw big. Use the whole page, on purpose, even if it means the drawing runs off the edge. Small drawings hide.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I watch tutorials or just draw?
output: Draw, mostly. A tutorial is worth it when you've hit a specific wall. Watching without drawing feels like learning and isn't.

subject: art_advice
input: Which YouTube channels are good for learning to draw?
output: Proko for figure and anatomy, Marco Bucci for painting and colour, Sinix for punchy fundamentals. There are loads, pick one and actually do the exercises.

subject: art_advice
input: Is art school worth it?
output: For some people. You get time, structure, people and access. You don't get anything you can't get elsewhere if you're disciplined. The debt is real.

subject: art_advice
input: Can I learn to draw for free?
output: Yes, entirely. Library books, YouTube, free pose sites, free software. The only thing you have to pay is time.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I learn from books or videos?
output: Both work. Books are slower and stick better. Videos show the hand moving. Loomis and Bridgman for books, then whoever you like watching.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I know if I'm improving?
output: Date your drawings and look back every three months. You won't see it week to week. Over months it's obvious.

subject: art_advice
input: What should a beginner draw?
output: Things in front of you. A cup, your hand, a shoe. Then people, from life or photos. Not dragons yet, they'll come.

subject: art_advice
input: Is drawing talent or practice?
output: Practice. Some people start a bit ahead, then practice decides everything. The best artists you know drew more than everyone else.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I draw from life if I'm shy?
output: Cafés and trains. People look at phones, they don't notice. Start with the backs of heads. Nobody's ever been arrested for sketching.

subject: art_advice
input: I can copy but I can't draw from my head.
output: That's normal and it's a memory problem, not a skill problem. Draw something from reference, close it, draw it again from memory, compare. Repeat.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I learn colour theory?
output: Skip most of the theory. Do colour studies: pick a photo, paint it in six colours, small, in an hour. Twenty of those teaches more than a book.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I get better at composition?
output: Thumbnails. Ten of them before every piece. And study films, they pay people a fortune to compose frames.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I practise perspective without it being tedious?
output: Draw the room you're in. Then the street. Real places with real boxes. Grids of cubes are a means, not the point.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I improve at painting light?
output: Paint the same object under a lamp, then by a window, then outside. Three studies, same object. Light becomes a thing you see instead of a thing you know.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I focus on one medium?
output: For a while, yes. Long enough to get past the annoying stage. Then try others. Everything you learn in one carries to the rest.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I get out of my comfort zone?
output: Draw the thing you avoid. If you never draw hands, draw a page of hands. Every week, one thing you're bad at.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I make time to draw with a full-time job?
output: Twenty minutes, same time, every day. Lunch break or before bed. Small and certain beats big and maybe.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I draw what I see instead of what I know?
output: Turn the reference upside down. Your brain stops naming things and starts seeing shapes. Old trick, still works.

subject: art_advice
input: What's the fastest way to improve?
output: Draw from life, get feedback, fix the thing they said, repeat. Also draw more than you think is reasonable.

subject: art_advice
input: Is it worth doing a 100-day challenge?
output: If you'll finish it. Most people don't, and that's fine, but plan for the wall around day twenty.

subject: art_advice
input: Do I need expensive paper?
output: For practice, no. For watercolour, yes, cheap paper genuinely doesn't work. For everything else, cheap is fine until you're selling.

subject: art_advice
input: What's the best beginner drawing tablet?
output: A small or medium pen tablet from Wacom, Huion or XP-Pen. Any of them. The cheap one is fine.

subject: art_advice
input: Do I need an iPad Pro or is the normal iPad okay?
output: The normal one with a Pencil is fine. Pro is nicer, bigger and faster. Neither will make you draw better.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I buy a set of pencils?
output: A 2B, a 4B and an HB is a set. Buy them loose. The tins of twelve are mostly grades you'll never use.

subject: art_advice
input: What brushes do I need to start acrylics?
output: One flat, one round, one small round. Synthetic. That's it for a year.

subject: art_advice
input: What paints should I start watercolour with?
output: A small pan set with a dozen colours. Student grade is fine. Get decent paper, that matters more than the paint.

subject: art_advice
input: Do I need a lightbox?
output: No. A window in daylight does the same thing. If you end up inking a lot, a cheap LED one is nice.

subject: art_advice
input: Is a drawing glove worth it?
output: On a screen tablet, yes, it stops the smearing and the palm getting read as a touch. On paper, it keeps grease off. Cheap, so why not.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I upgrade my tablet?
output: Only if it's actually stopping you doing something. Better tools don't make better drawings. More drawings make better drawings.

subject: art_advice
input: Is a second monitor useful for art?
output: Yes. Reference on one, canvas on the other. The cheapest one you can find is plenty.

subject: art_advice
input: I feel like a fraud posting my art.
output: Everyone does. It never entirely goes away. Post anyway. The people who look confident are mostly just used to feeling like frauds.

subject: art_advice
input: I'm scared of ruining a good drawing by continuing.
output: Photograph it now, then keep going. If you ruin it you've still got the photo, and you'll have learned where the edge is.

subject: art_advice
input: I only like my art for about a day.
output: That's the gap between your taste and your skill. Your taste's ahead, which is what pulls the skill up. It's a good sign, honestly.

subject: art_advice
input: How do I stop overworking pieces?
output: Set a timer and stop when it goes. Or work on two at once so you can't fiddle with either for long. Or decide the last step before you start.

subject: art_advice
input: I get jealous of other artists.
output: Normal. Turn it into a study: what exactly do they do that you want? Then practise that thing. Jealousy's just a badly worded wish list.

subject: art_advice
input: I don't know what to draw.
output: Then draw the nearest object. The blank page problem is solved by any mark at all. What to draw next is easier once something's on the page.

subject: art_advice
input: Is it okay to draw for fun and not to improve?
output: More than okay. Improving isn't compulsory. Some of the best drawings are made by people who aren't trying.

subject: art_advice
input: Am I wasting my time drawing?
output: If you like doing it, no. Hours spent doing something you like aren't wasted. They're the point.

subject: art_advice
input: I keep abandoning projects halfway.
output: Make them smaller. Finish a tiny thing today. Finishing is a muscle and it's got weak. Build it back with small ones.

subject: art_advice
input: Should I delete my old art online?
output: No. It shows the path. And the people who saw it already saw it. Leave it, or archive it privately if it bothers you.

A: What's gouache?
B: Opaque watercolour. Dries matte, you can put light over dark.

output: Not really. The main surprise is it dries a different shade than it goes on, lighter for darks, darker for lights. You get used to it.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's gouache?
B: Opaque watercolour. Dries matte, you can put light over dark.
A: Can I mix it with normal watercolour?
output: Yes, happily. Same binder. People use watercolour for the washes and gouache for the opaque bits on top.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's a vanishing point?
B: Where parallel lines seem to meet on the horizon.
A: Can I have more than one?
output: Yes. Two for a corner view, three if you're looking up or down as well. One set of parallel lines gets one point.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's a vanishing point?
B: Where parallel lines seem to meet on the horizon.
A: Does it have to be on the page?
output: No, and often it's better off it. Points close together on the page make things look fish-eyed.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's foreshortening?
B: Drawing something pointing at the viewer so it looks shorter than it is.
A: Why is it so hard?
output: Because your brain knows the arm is long and fights you drawing it short. Measure it, don't trust what you know.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's foreshortening?
B: Drawing something pointing at the viewer so it looks shorter than it is.
A: How do I practise it?
output: Draw your own arm reaching at a mirror. Then boxes and cylinders at angles. Overlap is the key, the near bit covers the far bit.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is value in art?
B: How light or dark something is, ignoring colour.
A: Is it more important than colour?
output: For making things read, yes. A painting with right values and wrong colours still works. The other way round, it falls apart.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is value in art?
B: How light or dark something is, ignoring colour.
A: How do I practise it?
output: Greyscale studies. A sphere under a lamp, then an apple, then a face. Squint a lot.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What are complementary colours?
B: Opposites on the colour wheel, like blue and orange.
A: What happens if I mix them?
output: They dull each other down towards grey or brown. Useful for shadows, disastrous if you do it by accident.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What are complementary colours?
B: Opposites on the colour wheel, like blue and orange.
A: Should I use them together?
output: Yes, but let one win. A mostly blue picture with a bit of orange sings. Half and half just shouts.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's the rule of thirds?
B: Put the important bits on the lines of a three by three grid.
A: Do I always have to follow it?
output: No. It's a way to avoid dead centre. Once you know why it works, break it when you've got a reason.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's the rule of thirds?
B: Put the important bits on the lines of a three by three grid.
A: Does it work for portraits?

subject: follow_up_questions
input:

A: How long should each one take?

subject: follow_up_questions
input:

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's a clipping mask?
B: A layer that only shows where the layer below has paint.
A: What's it for?
output: Shading. Put your flat colour down, clip a layer above it, and your shadows can't spill over the edges.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's a clipping mask?
B: A layer that only shows where the layer below has paint.
A: Is it the same as alpha lock?
output: Nearly. Alpha lock does it on the same layer, clipping does it on a new one above. Clipping is safer because you can delete it.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:

output: Caravaggio. Black backgrounds, one hard light, figures jumping out of the dark.

subject: follow_up_questions

subject: follow_up_questions
input:

subject: follow_up_questions

subject: follow_up_questions

B: A hidden black and white image that hides parts of a layer.
A: Why not just erase?
output: Because a mask is undoable next week. Erasing is gone. Paint white on the mask and it's back.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's a monoprint?
B: A print you can only make once.
A: How do I make one?
output: Paint on a sheet of glass or acetate, lay paper on it, press with your hand or a spoon, peel. That's it.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's a linocut?
B: A design carved into lino, inked and printed.
A: Do I need a press?
output: No. A wooden spoon rubbed on the back of the paper works fine for small ones.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is contrapposto?
B: Standing with the weight on one leg so hips and shoulders tilt opposite ways.
A: Why does it look better?
output: Because that's how people actually stand. Straight and level looks like a soldier or a statue.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is atmospheric perspective?
B: Distant things look paler and bluer because of the air.
A: Does it happen indoors?
output: Barely. There's not enough air in a room. You can fake it, though, a bit less contrast on the far wall.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is a study?
B: A drawing made to learn something, not to be finished.
A: Should I post studies?
output: Yes, and say they're studies. People like seeing the working.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's a master study?
B: Copying a great painting to learn how they did it.
A: Is it okay to post one?
output: Yes, label it as a study of whoever it is. Don't crop their name out and call it yours.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's an underpainting?
B: A rough first layer that sets the values before colour.
A: What colour should it be?
output: Something earthy and muted. Burnt sienna's the classic. Or grey if you want no colour bias.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is glazing?
B: Thin transparent layers of paint over dry layers.
A: How long between layers?
output: Until it's properly dry. For oils that's days. Acrylic, twenty minutes.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is line weight?
B: How thick or dark a line is.
A: Where should lines be thicker?
output: Underneath things, in shadow, and where something's closer. Thin where light hits and further away.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is a portfolio?
B: A collection of your best work.
A: How many pieces?
output: Ten to twenty. Only your best. One weak piece drags the whole thing down.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is a portfolio?
B: A collection of your best work.
A: Should it have sketches in?
output: A few, if they're good and show how you think. Mostly finished work though.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is a commission?
B: A piece someone pays you to make.
A: Should I take a deposit?
output: Yes. Half up front is normal. It filters out the people who'd have vanished.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is a commission?
B: A piece someone pays you to make.
A: What if they don't like it?
output: That's what the sketch stage is for. Get approval on the rough before you finish. After that, changes cost.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is fan art?
B: Art of characters that belong to someone else.
A: Can I sell it?
output: Legally it's the owner's call and it varies. Most people do small runs and hope. It's a risk you take with your eyes open.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is pixel art?
B: Art made one pixel at a time at tiny sizes.
A: What size should I start at?
output: 32 by 32. Small enough to finish, big enough for a face.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is pixel art?
B: Art made one pixel at a time at tiny sizes.
A: Which app?
output: Aseprite if you'll pay a little. Otherwise Piskel in a browser is free.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is a storyboard?
B: Small drawings that plan a film shot by shot.
A: How detailed?
output: Stick figures are fine. It's about what's in frame and where the camera is, not pretty drawing.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's a sketch dump?
B: A batch of rough sketches posted together.
A: How many sketches?
output: Whatever fills a page nicely. Six to twenty. Nobody's counting.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's Krita?
B: A free painting program for desktop.
A: Is it as good as Photoshop?
output: For painting, yes. For photo editing and print work, Photoshop still wins. For free, nothing beats it.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's Procreate?
B: A drawing app for iPad.
A: Is there a PC version?
output: No. iPad only. On desktop, Krita or Clip Studio do a similar job.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What's a stabiliser?
B: A setting that smooths your strokes.
A: Should I use it all the time?
output: No. On for lineart, off for sketching. Too much and the line starts lagging behind your hand.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is a screen tablet?
B: A tablet with a screen you draw directly on.
A: Is it worth the money?
output: If you'll use it daily, yes. If you're not sure, a pen tablet does the same job for a fraction of the price.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is squash and stretch?
B: Squashing on impact, stretching in fast motion.
A: Does it work for realistic animation?
output: Subtly, yes. A little in the cheeks and the step. Overdo it and it's a cartoon.

subject: follow_up_questions
input:
A: What is onion skinning?
B: Seeing faint previous and next frames while you draw.
A: Does Procreate have it?
output: Yes, in the animation assist. Most animation apps do.
